newsitem.title: USA: American Air pilots prepare for possible strike.
newsitem.headline: American Air pilots prepare for possible strike.

text.p: American Airlines pilots began preparing Thursday for a possible strike in mid-February and union leaders said there was a 50 percent chance their escalating contract dispute would be decided with a walkout.

One day after both sides turned down binding arbitration and began a 30-day "cooling off" period before a strike or lockout can begin, hundreds of pilots met at a Dallas hotel to discuss their demands and strike preparation measures.

Union leaders said they want a negotiated solution but warned there was a firm chance of strike action starting Feb. 15 at the country's second largest airline, which is owned by Fort Worth-based AMR Corp.
"It is something we certainly don't want but there is a good chance ... Fifty-fifty is a good probability," one senior official close to the stalled negotiations said.
Jim Sovich, president of the Allied Pilots Association (APA), blamed American's management for the impasse and urged his rank-and-file to stand firm.
"We have travelled a long road together. With your continued efforts, we will get the contract we deserve," Sovich told members on a union hotline message.

More than 60 percent of American's pilots last week rejected a four-year labor contract which was tentatively agreed to last September after two years of talks, and the union has now drawn up a list of fresh demands.

They include pay raises of more than 11 percent over the next four years, options on 7.25 million company shares at a discount of $10 each, elimination of a two-tier pay structure and a guarantee that American will not use its commuter carrier American Eagle, which employs pilots of another union, to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

AMR management says its pilots are the highest paid in the industry and that the new demands would cripple the airline's ability to compete, threatening modest growth plans and a $6.5 billion contract to buy 103 jets from Boeing Co.

Chief Financial Officer Gerard Arpey has said the dispute threatens American's future. "We quite frankly are at a loss as to what to do next; accept a contract that would be at best uncompetitive vs. our principal competitors, or a possible cessation of operations. Two disastrous sort of alternatives."
An airline spokesman said letters were mailed out to its 88,000 employees on Thursday, warning them they might be put on indefinite leave without pay in the event of a strike. But
union leaders scoffed at Arpey's comments and pointed to AMR's announcement on Wednesday that it ran up record profits of $1.02 billion last year.

They insisted the APA's 9,300 pilots were unified and that they would shut the airline down entirely in any strike. There appeared to be little dissent among the hundreds of pilots at the Dallas meeting.
"The bottom line with pilots is that you do not want to be a scab. You have to have harmony in the cockpit so you do not scab," said one pilot with 15 years experience.
